what: A feature flag is a switch in your code that you flip at runtime, without a deploy. It decides who sees new behaviour: nobody, some tenants, a percentage, or everyone.
like: Like a dimmer switch on new lighting: wired in already, you turn it up slowly, and snap it off if something flickers.
why: Separates deploying code from releasing it to users
Lets you roll out gradually and turn off fast (kill switch)
Runs A/B experiments on real traffic

nodes.t: SDK in your app|rules kept in memory

steps.d: In the dashboard you set a rule, for example: tenants Acme and Globex get the new pipeline, plus 10% of everyone else.
The flag service pushes rule changes to every connected SDK. The SDK keeps the rules in an in-memory cache, so checks are local and fast.
Your code asks: is new-pipeline on for this context (tenant, user)? Targeted tenants match first; no network call is needed.
For a percentage, the SDK hashes the user or tenant key into a bucket. The same key always lands in the same bucket, so users do not flip-flop.
On sends the request to the new pipeline, off keeps the old one. Moving a tenant across is just a rule change.
Compare errors and latency per variant. Healthy: raise the percentage. Problems: flip the kill switch and everyone is back on the old path.

numbers.l: toggle kinds: release, experiment, ops, permission
buckets LaunchDarkly hashes contexts into for percentage rollouts
rollout steps can use up to three decimal places
OpenFeature accepted as a CNCF incubating project

choices.d: Release flags live days to weeks and then get deleted. Experiment flags last one test. Ops kill switches and permission flags can stay long-term, on purpose.
Bucket by tenant for B2B cutovers, so a whole company moves together. Bucket by user for consumer features and experiments.
For example 1%, 10%, 50%, 100%, pausing at each step to watch error rate and latency per variant.
Server SDKs evaluate in memory from streamed rules: fast and still working if the flag service is down. Client-side SDKs get pre-evaluated values to keep rules private.
Code against the OpenFeature API and plug in a provider (LaunchDarkly, Flagsmith, your own), so switching vendors does not touch every call site.

instead.why: Canary by traffic weight between two deployments, no code switch
Route whole tenants to a new backend at the gateway
Test a ranking change offline before any live traffic sees it

breaks.d: Old release flags stay in the code and nobody knows what they do.
breaks.see: Hundreds of flags, many at 100% for months
breaks.fix: Owner and expiry date per flag; delete code and config once fully rolled out

breaks.d: Bucketing uses a random number or a changing key.
breaks.see: Same user sees old then new UI; muddy experiment results
breaks.fix: Hash a stable key (user or tenant id)

breaks.d: Many flags interact in ways no one tried.
breaks.see: Bug appears only with two flags on together
breaks.fix: Few flags, few toggle points; test next-release flags on and all flags on

breaks.d: The SDK cannot fetch rules at startup.
breaks.fix: Safe default values in code, cached rules, local evaluation

say: We cut tenants over from the old pipeline to the new one with a feature flag targeted by tenant id, starting with internal and friendly tenants.
Server SDKs keep the rules in memory, so each check is a local lookup and the flag service is not on the request path.
For percentage steps I bucket by a hash of the tenant id, so a tenant stays on the same side, and I watch error rate and latency per variant.
Once every tenant is migrated, we delete the flag and the old code path so we do not build up flag debt.

followups.q: How does a percentage rollout stay consistent?
followups.a: The SDK hashes a stable key, such as the user or tenant id, into a fixed bucket. Raising the percentage only adds buckets, so people already on stay on.

A release flag hides unfinished work and goes away once launched. An experiment flag splits users into variants to measure an outcome, like click-through or answer quality, and ends when the test is decided.
A vendor-neutral, CNCF-hosted API for evaluating flags. Your code calls one standard API, and a provider plugs in the actual flag vendor or an in-house system.

followups.q: How would you test a new reranker this way?
followups.a: Put it behind an experiment flag, bucket queries or users by hash, and compare online metrics per variant after offline evals look good. Roll forward or flip back instantly.

today: OpenFeature, a vendor-neutral flag API, has been a CNCF incubating project since December 2023, so flag calls can stay the same if you switch vendors.

check.q: You need to turn off a misbehaving feature in seconds, without a deploy. Which flag type?
check.why: Ops toggles exist so operators can change behaviour at runtime instantly.

check.q: How should a 10% rollout pick users?
check.a: Hash a stable user or tenant id into buckets
d: Users whose name starts with A-C
check.why: Hashing a stable key gives each person the same answer every time.

check.q: Why do server SDKs evaluate flags in memory?
check.a: Fast checks with no network call per request
d: Because rules are secret from the server
To avoid needing a flag service at all
check.why: Rules stream in once and each check is a local lookup.

check.q: A release flag has been at 100% for six months. What now?
check.a: Remove the flag and the old code path
check.why: Retiring release flags avoids flag debt and untested paths.
